heading: Nginx Config Validator
tagline: Paste an nginx.conf and catch syntax errors, misplaced directives, and common security mistakes — before you reload nginx.

ui.dropHint: Drop a .conf file here, or paste config text above.
ui.privacyNote: Everything runs in your browser — your config is never uploaded to any server.
ui.regexPcreNote: Uses JavaScript's regex engine, not nginx's real PCRE engine — close, but not identical (e.g. no possessive quantifiers/atomic groups).
ui.rewriteReplacementLabel: Replacement (use $1, $2… or $name for captures; the whole URI is replaced, like nginx)
ui.rewriteNoMatch: Pattern does not match — rewrite would not apply.
ui.emptyState: Paste an nginx config above (or load the sample) and the checks will appear here.
ui.fragmentAutoNote: Allow top-level server, location, upstream… blocks (a file meant for include). This is also detected automatically when the config has no http, events, stream or mail block.
ui.regexTimeout: The pattern took too long to evaluate (possible catastrophic backtracking) and was stopped.
ui.regexWorkerError: The regex check failed to run.

issues.missing-semicolon: Directive "{{directive}}" is missing a terminating ";" before "}".
issues.missing-semicolon-eof: Directive "{{directive}}" is missing a terminating ";" (reached end of file).
issues.unclosed-block: Block "{{name}}" opened here is never closed with "}".
issues.possible-missing-semicolon: "{{directive}}" looks like it starts a new directive, but the previous line has no ";" — did you forget one after "{{previous}}"?
issues.wrong-context: "{{directive}}" is not valid inside the "{{context}}" block — valid in: {{allowed}}.
issues.crlf-injection-risk: "{{directive}}" uses "$uri" (URL-decoded) — an attacker-controlled decoded value here can inject characters into the response. Prefer "$request_uri" (raw, unaltered) for redirects/headers unless you specifically need the decoded form.
issues.autoindex-enabled: "autoindex on;" lists directory contents to any visitor when no index file exists — confirm this is intentional.
issues.server-tokens-exposed: No "server_tokens off;" found anywhere — nginx will expose its exact version number in the Server response header and default error pages, which helps an attacker target known CVEs for that version.
issues.unclosed-quote: Unclosed {{quote}} quote — the string started here never ends.
issues.unknown-directive: Unknown directive "{{directive}}" — not a standard nginx directive (a third-party module may define it).
issues.unknown-directive-suggest: Unknown directive "{{directive}}" — did you mean "{{suggestion}}"? (A third-party module may define it.)
issues.weak-ssl-protocol: "ssl_protocols" enables the obsolete protocol {{protocol}} — it has known attacks; allow only TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3.
issues.alias-traversal: Location "{{location}}" does not end with "/" but uses alias — a request like "{{location}}../" can reach files outside the aliased directory (path traversal). End both the location and the alias path with "/".
issues.add-header-redefine: "add_header" here replaces ALL add_header values inherited from the parent block (line {{parentLine}}). Missing in this block: {{names}}.
issues.proxy-set-header-redefine: "proxy_set_header" here replaces ALL proxy_set_header values inherited from the parent block (line {{parentLine}}). Missing in this block: {{names}}.
issues.if-in-location: "if" inside a location is unreliable when it contains {{directives}}; only return, rewrite and set are safe there. Use map, try_files or separate locations instead.
issues.missing-hsts: This TLS server never sends a Strict-Transport-Security header. Add: add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
issues.allow-without-deny: "allow" without "deny all;" in the same block restricts nothing — addresses that match no rule are allowed by default.
issues.proxy-pass-uri-regex: nginx rejects "proxy_pass" with a URI part ("/…") inside a regex location, named location, "if" or "limit_except". Remove the URI or use a variable.
issues.status-page-exposed: "stub_status" exposes live connection counters to anyone who can reach this location. Restrict it with allow/deny or auth_basic.
issues.root-in-location: "root" is set inside location "{{location}}". Prefer one "root" at server level; per-location roots are easy to get wrong (compare with alias).
issues.valid-referers-none: "valid_referers none" also accepts requests that send no Referer header, so the check is trivially bypassed.
issues.duplicate-default-server: A second "default_server" for {{listen}} (first one at line {{line}}) — nginx refuses to start.
issues.duplicate-server-name: server_name "{{name}}" on {{listen}} is already used by the server at line {{line}}; nginx ignores this one ("conflicting server name").
issues.upstream-undeclared: "{{directive}}" points at "{{name}}", which is not declared as an upstream block in this file (ignore this if it is a real host name).
issues.param-invalid-size: "{{directive}}" must be a size such as 512, 64k or 10m (got "{{value}}").
issues.param-invalid-time: "{{directive}}" must be a time such as 30s, 5m or 1h (got "{{value}}").
issues.listen-invalid-port: "listen {{value}}": the port must be a number between 1 and 65535.
issues.return-invalid-code: "return {{code}}" is not valid: use an HTTP status code (100-599) or a full URL.
issues.return-needs-url: "return {{code}}" is a redirect and needs a target URL as the second argument.
issues.error-page-invalid: "error_page": "{{value}}" is not a valid error code (300-599).

faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: No. `nginx -t` is the only tool that checks your config against the exact nginx build and modules actually installed on your server, and it's the final word before a reload. This validator catches the same class of mistakes (syntax errors, wrong directive placement, a handful of security smells) before you even get to a server with nginx installed — useful while editing locally, in a CI step, or when you don't have shell access to the target machine yet.
faq.a2: No — it covers a small, deliberately chosen set of checks (missing `server_tokens off;`, `autoindex on;`, and `$uri` used where `$request_uri` is safer) loosely inspired by Gixy, the open-source nginx config auditor. It is not a replacement for Gixy or a full security audit.
faq.q3: Why does the regex tester behave slightly differently from real nginx?
faq.a3: nginx's `location ~` and `location ~*` matching uses PCRE (via the bundled PCRE library in the nginx binary). This tool runs entirely in your browser, so it uses JavaScript's built-in RegExp engine instead — the two are very close for common patterns, but PCRE-only features like possessive quantifiers or atomic groups won't behave the same way here.
faq.q4: Does my config ever leave my browser?
faq.a4: No. Parsing, validation, and both simulators run with plain JavaScript in this tab. Nothing is uploaded, logged, or sent anywhere — you can even disconnect from the internet after the page loads and it keeps working.

article.heading: Catching nginx config mistakes before they reach production
article.p1: A broken nginx.conf usually announces itself in one of two unpleasant ways: `nginx -t` refusing to reload with a cryptic line-number error, or — worse — a `reload` silently keeping the old (working) config in memory while the new one sits broken on disk, so nothing seems wrong until the next full restart. Both are avoidable by catching the same class of mistakes earlier, while you're still editing.
article.p2: The most common real-world nginx.conf mistake isn't exotic — it's a forgotten semicolon. Because nginx's grammar only cares about `;`, `{`, and `}` (not line breaks), a missing `;` doesn't produce a clean "line 12: expected ;" error the way most modern parsers do; instead, the next directive's name and arguments silently get absorbed as extra arguments of the previous directive, sometimes with no error at all until something downstream behaves strangely. This tool's line-break heuristic specifically watches for that pattern — a known directive name appearing mid-argument-list on a new source line — and flags it before it becomes a support ticket.
article.p3: Directive placement is the second common trap: `proxy_pass` only makes sense inside a `location` (or `if`) block, `listen`/`server_name` only inside `server`, and so on — but nginx's own parser doesn't reject a directive just because it's in an unusual place if the directive name is one it recognizes at all in a broader sense, and error messages are pointed at nginx's own internal directive registry rather than at "you nested this wrong." This validator checks the directive-to-context table directly, so a `proxy_pass` accidentally left at the `http` level (outside any `server`/`location`) gets flagged with the exact line, not just "the config failed to load."
article.p4: Beyond syntax, a handful of small config choices have outsized security consequences: leaving `server_tokens` at its default (`on`) hands out your exact nginx version in every response header and default error page, which is free reconnaissance for anyone probing for a version-specific CVE; using the URL-decoded `$uri` variable inside a `return`/`rewrite`/`add_header` (instead of the raw `$request_uri`) can let an attacker inject characters into a redirect target under some configurations. Neither of these breaks anything visibly during normal testing, which is exactly why they're worth a dedicated pass rather than relying on noticing them by eye in a 200-line config.
